section.title: A Better Covenant
section.sectionRationale: The writer sums up his argument so far: we have a high priest seated in heaven, ministering in the true sanctuary. The earthly system was only a copy and shadow. Christ mediates a better covenant, and the writer proves the old was always meant to give way by quoting Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on the heart, with sins remembered no more.
section.thesis: Christ is the high priest seated in heaven who serves in the true tabernacle, and He mediates a better covenant founded on better promises; the very fact that God promised a new covenant through Jeremiah, one of inward transformation, universal knowledge of God, and complete forgiveness, shows the first covenant was provisional and is now passing away.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the summary of Christ's heavenly ministry in the true sanctuary, of which the earthly was a copy and shadow; and the citation of Jeremiah's new covenant, proving the first obsolete and introducing the better one.

units.label: A high priest in the true sanctuary

verses.text: The point of what we are saying is this: We do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven,
and who ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man.
And since every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices, it was necessary for this One also to have something to offer.
Now if He were on earth, He would not be a priest, since there are already priests who offer gifts according to the law.

The place where they serve is a copy and {{skia|shadow}} of what is in heaven. This is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”

units.label: The better covenant of Jeremiah
units.note: written on the heart, sins remembered no more

verses.text: Now, however, Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, just as the {{diatheke|covenant}} He {{mesites|mediates}} is {{kreitton|better}} and is founded on better promises.
For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second.
But God found fault with the people and said: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.

It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not abide by My covenant, and I disregarded them, declares the Lord.

For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.
No longer will each one teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.
For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.”
By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete; and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear.

skia.gloss: A shadow, a shadowy outline cast by a solid reality. The earthly tabernacle and its worship were a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary, real yet provisional, pointing to the substance that has come in Christ.

diatheke.gloss: A covenant, a binding arrangement established by God. The word can also mean a will or testament. Christ mediates a new and better covenant, founded on better promises, which supersedes the first.

mesites.gloss: A mediator, the one who stands between two parties to establish and maintain an agreement. Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant, His own ministry securing its better promises for God's people.

kreitton.gloss: Better, superior, more excellent. A keyword of the letter: the covenant Christ mediates is better, resting on better promises, because it accomplishes inwardly what the first could only picture.

basic.context: The writer sums up his case: we have a high priest who is seated at God's right hand and serves in the true, heavenly sanctuary, not a man-made tent. The earthly tabernacle was only a copy and shadow of the real one. Christ's ministry is far greater because the covenant He mediates is better. To prove the old covenant was always meant to pass, the writer quotes Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant of changed hearts and full forgiveness.
basic.hermeneutics: Notice the two arguments: from the sanctuary, earthly is a shadow of heavenly; and from Jeremiah, the very promise of a new covenant shows the first was not final. Read Jeremiah 31 as God's own testimony that the old was provisional.
basic.originalLanguages: The earthly system is a skia, shadow, of heaven. Jesus mediates a diathēkē, covenant, as its mesitēs, mediator, and this covenant is kreittōn, better, founded on better promises.
basic.typology: The tabernacle Moses built by the heavenly pattern is a shadow of the true sanctuary where Christ ministers. The old covenant itself foreshadows the new, which fulfills what it could only point toward.
basic.christ: Christ is the seated high priest in the true tabernacle and the mediator of the better covenant. His ministry secures inward transformation, knowledge of God, and complete forgiveness that the old covenant only promised.
basic.god: God found fault not with His covenant's holiness but with the people's failure, and He Himself promised a new covenant. It is God who writes His law on hearts, gives knowledge of Himself, and forgives sins, remembering them no more.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 31 is the quoted promise. Exodus 25 gives the pattern on the mountain. Luke 22 records Jesus naming the new covenant in His blood.
basic.oneStory: The old covenant always pointed beyond itself; God promised a new one, and in Christ that new covenant of transformed hearts and forgiven sins has come.

context.literary:
Verse 1 announces itself: 'The point of what we are saying is this.' The Greek word behind 'point' can mean the main thing or the sum, and the writer is telling readers that the long exposition of chapters 5 to 7 has been leading to one affirmation, a high priest seated in heaven. From there the chapter makes two moves that interlock. Verses 1 to 6 argue from place: the true sanctuary is in heaven and the earthly tent was modelled on it. Verses 7 to 13 argue from time: God's own promise of a new covenant shows the first one was never meant to be the last.

The two halves are joined by the word 'covenant' in verse 6, which acts as a hinge. Before it, the discussion is about priesthood and sanctuary. After it, the discussion is about the arrangement between God and His people that priesthood and sanctuary served. Verse 6 also repeats the comparative 'better' twice, a word the writer has used again and again, and it names the grounds: a more excellent ministry, a better covenant, better promises.

The center of the chapter is a long quotation, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, introduced as God's own speech, 'declares the Lord', and it is the longest quotation of the Old Testament in the New. The writer does not interrupt it. He lets the whole oracle stand, and then comments with a single sentence in verse 13. The quotation itself has a clear shape: a promise of a new covenant, a contrast with the old, three provisions beginning with 'I will', and a final 'for' clause that grounds the others in forgiveness. The writer reuses the same quotation in an abridged form in Hebrews 10:16 and 17, so it frames the whole teaching on sacrifice between them.
context.historical:
Jeremiah spoke these words in the shadow of the fall of Jerusalem, in a section of his book often called the Book of Consolation, Jeremiah 30 to 33. The nation had broken the covenant made at Sinai, and Jeremiah himself had preached against it, as in Jeremiah 11:1 to 8. Yet in the same period God promised restoration, and this oracle is the high point. It is striking that a prophet whose message was judgment is the one who announces a covenant that will not fail.

For the first hearers of Hebrews, the words had practical weight. The temple was still the centre of national life, and a Jewish Christian under pressure could hear the question: why leave a covenant established by Moses for a movement that lacks a priesthood, a sanctuary, a cult? The writer answers from within the Scriptures. Jeremiah himself called the Sinai covenant a covenant that Israel broke, and he spoke of the coming days when God would do something new. That the old arrangement had always carried the seeds of its own replacement is the conviction that Jeremiah's hearers should have taken.

The promise 'they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest', verse 11, addresses a society in which knowledge of God was mediated by priests, prophets and teachers. It does not say teaching ends; it says that every member of the covenant people will have the knowledge and not only the privileged few. Verse 5 reminds readers that Moses was told to build 'according to the pattern shown you on the mountain', which is Exodus 25:40, and that the first temple builders had the same assurance, 1 Chronicles 28:19. Both were copies of a pattern, and the writer builds his case on that assurance.
context.canonical:
The new covenant is a thread that begins before Jeremiah and runs to the end of the Bible. The Torah itself had spoken of a heart problem and its cure: Deuteronomy 30:6 says that the LORD 'will circumcise your hearts', so the inward work promised by Jeremiah was already present in Moses. Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 says the same in other words, with a new heart and the gift of God's Spirit, and Ezekiel 37:26 speaks of an everlasting covenant of peace. Isaiah 42:6 and 49:8 hear the LORD appoint His Servant 'to be a covenant for the people', which prepares for the idea that a person, and not only a document, can be the covenant.

Jesus takes the phrase into His own mouth at the table. In Luke 22:20 He says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood', and Paul passes on the same words in 1 Corinthians 11:25. In 2 Corinthians 3:3 and 6 Paul speaks of ministers of a new covenant, a letter written 'not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts', which is Jeremiah's picture and Sinai's tablets together.

Within Hebrews the quotation returns. Hebrews 10:15 to 18 reuses its last two lines and adds, 'where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed', and Hebrews 12:24 and 13:20 name Jesus as mediator of a new covenant and speak of 'the blood of the eternal covenant'. Jeremiah 31:35 to 37 follows the oracle and ties it to God's fixed order of sun, moon and stars, and Romans 11:27 echoes the promise with 'when I take away their sins', which is why Paul can still speak of God's purposes for Israel while preaching the gospel.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his readers to hear the Old Testament speaking against their instinct to go back to it. The instinct is understandable. A covenant given by God at Sinai carries real authority, and anyone who loves Scripture will want to honour it. He does not argue against Moses. He argues from Jeremiah, one of their own prophets, that God Himself said the first arrangement would be succeeded. His sentence in verse 7 is the key: 'if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second.' If God was still seeking a second, the first was not the end.

He also means readers to take heart rather than fear. The new covenant is described through verbs of God's action: 'I will put', 'I will be', 'I will forgive.' None of these depends on the people's performance, which is exactly what failed under the first covenant, verse 9. So the passage is not only a refutation, it is a promise to a tired and wavering people that the thing they cannot do for themselves, God has pledged to do.

Finally, he intends the reader to see the link between heaven and the work of the priest. The sanctuary is not a symbol of a doctrine; it is where Christ is serving now. The point is that the ministry of Jesus is current and real, which is why it can secure what the old ministry could not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage describes what God has done and promised. It does not command a program. When it says 'they will all know Me', it is not saying teaching or preaching is pointless, since the same letter urges readers to encourage one another and to remember their leaders, Hebrews 3:13 and 13:7. Reading verse 11 as a ban on instruction misreads a promise about the common knowledge of God for a rule against teachers.

The same care applies to verse 13, which says what is 'obsolete and aging will soon disappear'. This is not a license to despise the Old Testament, to treat Moses as irrelevant or to ignore the law's moral witness. The writer is speaking of the covenant arrangement, with its priesthood and sacrifices, which has been fulfilled. The same Old Testament is the writer's authority throughout, and he takes it as binding on how to read Christ.

What carries forward is confidence and direction. Believers live under a covenant in which God's law is not external and forgiveness is not partial, so obedience can be seen as a response of the heart and not a ladder to climb. Jeremiah's own emphasis on 'laws in their minds' means the content of what God wants is not cancelled, only internalised, a point Paul makes in Romans 8:3 and 4.

debates.question: In what sense is the first covenant 'at fault' and 'obsolete'?

views.label: Provisional and superseded, not evil
views.case: Verse 8 says God 'found fault with the people', which shifts the blame to those who did not abide in the covenant, verse 9. The covenant was holy and good, but it was preparatory, a copy and shadow, verse 5. It is obsolete because what it pointed to has come, in the way a scaffold becomes unnecessary once the building is finished.

views.label: Inherently unable to change hearts
views.case: Others stress verse 7, 'if that first covenant had been without fault', and Hebrews 7:18, 'weak and useless'. On this view the arrangement itself lacked a built-in remedy for the heart. It could expose sin and provide ritual cleansing, but it could not write the law within or give final forgiveness. The new covenant supplies what the old was structurally unable to give.

views.label: The fault is in the people, but the weakness is real
views.case: A middle reading holds both statements together: the covenant was good and the people failed, yet the covenant's terms, with a mediator who dies and sacrifices that repeat, left the failure uncured. The Greek of verse 8 says God found fault 'with them', which supports the blame on the people, while verse 7 speaks of the covenant itself.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the first covenant was given by God and was holy in its place, and that holding to it now, after Christ, misses what it was for. The difference is whether the stress falls on the people's failing or on the arrangement's limits, which Hebrews seems to hold together.

debates.question: To whom does the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 apply?

views.label: The church, as the new covenant people of God
views.case: Hebrews quotes the promise 'with the house of Israel' and applies it to the readers, Jewish and Gentile believers in Christ. Luke 22:20, 2 Corinthians 3:6 and Hebrews 10:15 to 18 take it as fulfilled in Christ's people. The church is thus treated as the community into which the promise has come.

views.label: Israel and the church together, in the one people of God
views.case: Paul says Gentiles are grafted into Israel's own tree, Romans 11:17 to 24, and that Christ makes Jew and Gentile one, Ephesians 2:12 to 19. The covenant is made with Israel and Judah, and Gentiles share it by union with the Israelite Messiah, so there is one covenant and one people.

views.label: Fulfilled in the church now, with a future for national Israel
views.case: Some see an initial fulfilment in the church and a further one when Israel turns to the Lord, pointing to Romans 11:26 and 27, which echoes Jeremiah's 'when I take away their sins.' They read Jeremiah's own context, with its land and its city, as still carrying a hope for the nation.

debates.bearing: The writer of Hebrews applies the promise to his readers without hesitation, and every view keeps that. The disagreement lies in what remains for ethnic Israel, which Hebrews does not discuss and Romans 9 to 11 must be read to answer.

study.originalLanguages:
The writer calls Christ a leitourgos, a 'minister', of the sanctuary, verse 2, and the ministry He has received a leitourgia, verse 6. These are the words of public service, used in the Greek Old Testament for the work of priests and Levites at the tent, and the same family gives us the word 'liturgy'. Calling Christ a leitourgos puts Him at work in the sanctuary now, in a continuing service and not a completed one. The sanctuary in which He serves is the 'true' tent, alethine, a word that here means the real as against the copy, and not the true as against the false.

Verse 5 calls the earthly furniture a hypodeigma and a skia. The first word means a sketch or example, something that shows how a thing is done. The writer then quotes Exodus 25:40, where the Greek says Moses was shown a typos, a 'pattern' or mould, and the Hebrew word is tabnit, a model. These are three words for the relationship between earthly and heavenly: model, shadow, pattern. The earthly tent is real and God-given, and it is derived. Hebrews does not say it is unreal.

Verse 6 says the new covenant 'is founded on better promises', and the Greek verb is nenomothetetai, literally 'has been legislated' or 'enacted', from nomos, law. The new covenant is not a loose arrangement but an enacted one, with a legal basis. The perfect tense stresses that it stands in force. The comparison 'better', kreitton, appears throughout Hebrews, but the writer says the promises are better, which is the surprise, since the old covenant also contained promises. The difference turns out to be that these promises are God's unilateral 'I will' commitments.

In verse 7 the old covenant is amemptos, 'without fault', and verse 8 says God 'found fault', memphomai. The two words share the root meaning blame, and the writer plays on them. The Greek of verse 8 can read 'finding fault with them', which fits the people being blamed, as the quotation says.

The quotation brings out several points. 'New' in verses 8 and 13 is kainos, new in kind or quality, not neos, merely recent. The Hebrew of Jeremiah says God 'cuts' a covenant, karat, the standard idiom from the cutting of animals. In verse 9, 'I disregarded them' follows the Greek Old Testament, which reads emelesa, 'I neglected'; the Hebrew of Jeremiah 31:32 has a verb that can mean 'I was their husband' or 'I was lord over them', so translators differ, and the writer is using the form his readers had. Verse 10 says 'I will put My laws', plural, where Jeremiah has the singular torah, and the Greek lists laws in the mind and on the heart. Verse 11 has two different words for knowing, ginosko in the command 'Know the Lord' and oida in the promise 'they will all know Me', and the second suggests an intimate acquaintance. Verse 12 says God will be 'merciful', hileos, toward their iniquities, which is the adjective behind the word for the mercy seat, hilasterion, in Hebrews 9:5.

Verse 13 has the participle 'in speaking of a new', and the BSB footnote says the word 'covenant' is not in the Greek, so the writer's phrase is wider, and some read it to take in priesthood and tabernacle as well. He then says the first has been 'made obsolete', pepalaioken, literally 'made old', and is 'aging', gerasko, and near 'disappearance', aphanismos. The verbs are present and perfect: a thing already declared old and in the process of vanishing.

typology.type: The tabernacle built after the pattern on the mountain, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Moses was told to make everything 'according to the pattern shown you on the mountain', Exodus 25:40. The earthly tent is therefore a copy made from a heavenly original, and Hebrews calls it a shadow. The fulfilment is that Christ now serves in the original, the 'true tabernacle', verse 2, which God and not man has set up. Jesus entered heaven itself, Hebrews 9:24. The type is not false: its function was to teach, and the pattern's purposes were met. It falls short in that a copy cannot be inhabited with the fullness of the Presence, and its priests stood while Christ sat down, as Hebrews 10:11 and 12 contrast.

typology.type: Moses as mediator of the old covenant
typology.fulfillment: Moses stood between God and Israel, brought the words of the law down the mountain and sprinkled the covenant blood, Exodus 24:3 to 8. Hebrews 3:5 says he was faithful as a servant in God's house, 'testifying to what would be spoken later', and Jesus is the Son over the house. Christ mediates a covenant in which God's own promises carry the weight. The correspondence is of role, one man standing between two parties, but it grows: Moses mediated a covenant the people broke, while Christ mediates a covenant whose terms God Himself keeps, verse 10.

typology.type: The law written on stone becomes the law written on hearts
typology.fulfillment: The tablets of stone at Sinai, inscribed by the finger of God, Exodus 31:18, stand for a law outside the people. Jeremiah promises that God will 'inscribe them on their hearts', verse 10, and Paul takes it that the Corinthians themselves are a letter written 'on tablets of human hearts', 2 Corinthians 3:3. The new covenant is the same law in a new place, with the Spirit providing the power. The type falls short in that stone could show the standard but could not change anyone, and the stone had nothing to say to a person's hidden desires.

typology.type: The covenant sealed in blood as the pattern of a better covenant
typology.fulfillment: The old covenant was put into effect with blood, as Exodus 24:8 records, and the new covenant arrives with its own, which Jesus names at the supper, Luke 22:20. Zechariah 9:11 had already spoken of 'the blood of My covenant' as the means of releasing prisoners. The escalation is from the blood of animals to the blood of the Son, and from a ceremony that marked a people to a death that removes sin. The pattern is partial: the first covenant's blood could set apart and cleanse outwardly, while this covenant's blood is said to secure the forgiveness of verse 12.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by naming His present position before it describes any of His past work. The first verse says we have a high priest who 'sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven'. The writer has taken the royal seat of Psalm 110:1 and set a priest on it, so that the priest who serves is also the king who reigns. A seated priest is a surprise, since priests in the tabernacle never sat; there were no chairs in the tent, and their work was never done. Hebrews 10:11 and 12 draws the contrast explicitly, but the clue is already here.

The chapter also says what Christ must have: 'it was necessary for this One also to have something to offer', verse 3. That sentence guards against a vague idea of a spiritual priest who needs no sacrifice. The next chapters say what He offered. The writer says here only that the offering exists, and that He could not serve on earth, verse 4, since He is not of the tribe that serves there. That is not a defect. Because He is from Judah, His ministry is elsewhere, in the sanctuary that the earthly priests only copied.

Verse 6 says He has received a ministry 'much more excellent', and that He mediates a better covenant. Jeremiah promised the covenant, but a promise needs someone to enact it. Christ is the one who does, and Hebrews says He does it by His death, 9:15. Luke 22:20 shows Jesus claiming this role on the night He was betrayed, 'the new covenant in My blood', and 1 Timothy 2:5 calls Him the one mediator between God and men.

Each of the three provisions in the quotation is tied to Christ in the wider New Testament. The law written on the heart is the work of the Spirit whom Christ sends, John 14:26 and 2 Corinthians 3:3. The knowledge of God, from the least to the greatest, is given 'in the face of Christ', and Jesus says that no one knows the Father except through the Son, Matthew 11:27. The remembering of sins no more is secured by His cross: Hebrews 10:17 and 18 says that where sins are forgiven, an offering is no longer needed.

Verse 13 is not a boast against the old. It is the confirmation that what the first covenant promised, the second has delivered in Him. The old was a pointer and the new has arrived, and the One who delivers it is the same Lord who gave the first. This is why the old covenant must not be read as a failed experiment. The writer sees one plan, with Christ in view from the start.

A word of caution applies. Not every feature of the tabernacle is a coded picture of Jesus. The writer himself says the earthly tent was a copy of the heavenly, and he speaks of its function, not of every curtain and clasp. The links worth drawing are the ones the New Testament draws, and the chapter's main contribution is that the heavenly priest is serving now.
study.god:
God is the speaker throughout the quotation, and the repeated phrase 'declares the Lord' marks every stage. What the chapter shows first is a God who takes the initiative. 'I will make a new covenant', 'I will put', 'I will be', 'I will forgive.' In the first covenant the people had said 'We will do all that the LORD has spoken', Exodus 24:7, and in the second the grammar shifts to what God says He will do. The covenant of the heart is grace from beginning to end, which is why it can succeed where the other did not.

The chapter shows a God who is honest about failure. Verse 8 says God found fault with the people, and verse 9 says they 'did not abide' in the covenant. He does not blame the covenant He gave, and He does not soften the people's guilt. But He does not abandon His purpose either. The text sets a diagnosis beside a remedy: because the people did not stay, God will give them hearts that do. His faithfulness is not suspended on their faithfulness, which is also the message of Jeremiah 31:35 to 37, where God ties His promise to the fixed order of creation.

The chapter shows a God who wants to be known and not only obeyed. The refrain 'I will be their God, and they will be My people', verse 10, is the oldest covenant formula, from Leviticus 26:12 and Exodus 6:7. Here it is set beside the promise that all will know Him. The deepest purpose of the covenant is relationship, with the law as its shape and not its substitute.

It shows a God who forgives without pretending. Verse 12 says He will be merciful toward iniquities and 'will remember their sins no more.' This does not mean God loses information. In the Old Testament, to remember is to act on, as when God remembered Noah or remembered His covenant, and not to remember is not to act against. The sins will not be brought up against His people. How that can be just is the question the next chapters of Hebrews answer with the blood of Christ, since God does not simply wave the matter away.

It shows a God who designs in advance and builds in stages. The earthly tent was made after a pattern, and the promise of a new covenant was given before it was needed. God's plans are not improvised, and His earlier gifts are not mistakes. They are real and they are preparatory, which is a way of saying He is both patient and purposeful.

For worship, the chapter invites us to praise a God who does the inward work. We do not have to produce a new heart. We can ask the God who promised one to give it, and we can come to Him as people who are known and whose record has been closed.

crossReferences.note: The oracle the writer quotes almost in full. Its setting is the Book of Consolation, where God promises a covenant that exile cannot break. Reading it in Jeremiah shows that the three promises of law within, knowledge of God, and forgiveness were there from the start, and that Hebrews adds the one who secures them.

God asks for a sanctuary so that He may dwell among the people, and tells Moses to make it according to the pattern He will show. The text lays out the double truth Hebrews works from: the tent is real and given by God, and it is made after something else.

The ratification of the first covenant. The people promise to do all the LORD has spoken, Moses sprinkles the blood, and the covenant is sealed. It shows how readily the people pledged what they could not keep, which is the failure verse 9 describes, and it is the pattern Jesus echoes at the supper.

Moses himself promises that the LORD will circumcise their hearts so that they love Him. This shows the new covenant's inward work was foretold within the Torah, so that Jeremiah's promise is the fuller statement of something Moses already hoped for.

A parallel promise in Ezekiel: a new heart, a new spirit, and God's Spirit placed within so that His people walk in His statutes. It supplies the Spirit as the means by which the law is written within, which Jeremiah's wording leaves unstated.

Jesus at the last supper names the cup 'the new covenant in My blood'. It is the moment the promise of Jeremiah is claimed as His own, and it shows that the covenant is enacted by His death and not by teaching alone.

Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant, a letter written by the Spirit on human hearts and not on stone. It is the nearest New Testament parallel to Hebrews 8:10, and it shows the apostolic church read Jeremiah's promise as already being fulfilled.

The writer returns to the same quotation and cites its last lines, ending with 'an offering for sin is no longer needed.' It shows where he was heading all along: the forgiveness of the new covenant makes the old sacrifices redundant.

Says that after providing purification for sins, the Son sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. The wording is the same as 8:1, and it shows the seated priest was part of the letter's opening claim, not an afterthought.

Paul links 'when I take away their sins' to the covenant promise to Israel, drawn from the same oracle in Isaiah and Jeremiah. It shows the promise of forgiveness still being held out to Israel and ties Hebrews' reading to Paul's wider hope.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opened with a God who walked with His creatures, and the Bible's long story is the story of a broken relationship being remade. The covenants are the steps. With Noah God promised to preserve the creation, with Abraham to bless the nations, at Sinai to make a people for Himself, and with David to establish a king. Each is real and each is a stage. Under Moses the people were given a law, a sanctuary and priests, and the promise 'I will be your God, and you will be My people' was lived out in a tent at the centre of the camp.

But the story kept running into the same wall. The people who pledged obedience at Sinai made a golden calf within weeks, and the long history of Judges, Kings and the prophets is the record of a covenant being broken by the people, not by God. The exile was the covenant curse arriving, as Deuteronomy had warned. And yet in the middle of the ruin, Jeremiah heard a promise that the covenant would be made again, and made in such a way that it could not be broken: law within, knowledge for all, sins no more remembered. Ezekiel heard the same of a new heart and a new spirit.

Hebrews 8 says that the promise has arrived in Jesus. He is the priest who sits in the heavenly sanctuary that Moses' tent copied, and He is the mediator who has enacted the better covenant. What is being done in Christ is not a departure from the story but its answer. The people who could not keep the law are given the Spirit who writes it within. The people who needed priests to teach them are now each given the knowledge of God. The people whose sins were remembered each year have their sins remembered no more.

The story still has a horizon. The new covenant is real now, and believers are described as having a heart in which God's law is written, but the full promise of 'they will all know Me' belongs to a time when no one will need to say 'Know the Lord'. Revelation 21:3 closes the circle: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.' The covenant formula of Sinai and Jeremiah reaches its last line there. The shadow gives way to the substance, and the pattern on the mountain becomes a city in which God lives with His people.

quiz.q: What was the earthly tabernacle in relation to heaven?

options.text: A copy and shadow of the true, heavenly sanctuary.
options.note: Verse 5 describes it as a copy and shadow built by the heavenly pattern.

options.text: The ultimate dwelling of God, needing no fulfillment.
options.note: It was provisional, a shadow of the greater reality.
It was God-ordained and meaningful, yet only a shadow.

options.text: A God-given sanctuary where He truly met with Israel.
options.note: True, God did dwell there, yet the passage's point is that it was only a copy and shadow of the heavenly reality.

quiz.q: How does the writer prove the first covenant was not final?

options.text: God Himself promised a new covenant through Jeremiah.
options.note: Verses 8 to 12 quote Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant.

options.text: The people simply grew tired of it.
options.note: It was God's promise of a new covenant, not mere weariness, that proved the point.

options.text: The prophets never mentioned any covenant.
options.note: Jeremiah explicitly foretold a new covenant.

options.text: The first covenant is called obsolete and aging.
options.note: This is stated in verse 13, but the proof the writer gives is that God Himself promised a new covenant through Jeremiah.

quiz.q: What are the key promises of the new covenant in Jeremiah?

options.text: God's law written on the heart, all knowing God, and sins remembered no more.
A larger temple and more sacrifices.
options.note: The new covenant is inward and forgiving, not more external ritual.
The promises are spiritual: transformed hearts and forgiveness, not merely political.

options.text: God being their God and they being His people.
options.note: This is genuinely part of the promise in verse 10, but the fullest answer includes the inward law, universal knowledge of God, and complete forgiveness.

quiz.q: Where does the new covenant find fault?

options.text: With the people who broke the first covenant, prompting God to promise a better one.
options.note: Verse 8 says God found fault with the people.
The fault was with the people, not with God or His holiness.

options.text: With the very idea of any covenant.
options.note: God affirms covenant by promising a new one, not by rejecting the concept.

options.text: With the first covenant, which could not make anyone perfect.
options.note: The first covenant was indeed weak, but verse 8 specifies that God found fault with the people who broke it.

questions: The new covenant writes God's law on the heart. How is that different from merely following external rules, and where do you see it at work in you?
God promises to remember our sins no more. What would change if you truly believed your forgiven sins are gone from God's memory?
Christ ministers for us in the true sanctuary in heaven. How does His present, ongoing ministry encourage you today?
The old covenant was a shadow pointing to Christ. Are there religious shadows you cling to instead of resting in the substance He provides?
In the new covenant, all God's people know Him, from the least to the greatest. How does that shape the way you value every believer's relationship with God?

translationNotes.note: The quotation is Jeremiah 31:31-34, the longest Old Testament citation in the New Testament; the writer follows the Septuagint wording closely.
'Covenant' translates diathēkē, which can also mean a will or testament; the writer will exploit both senses in chapter 9.
'Obsolete and aging' pictures the first covenant as a worn garment near its end; the writer, likely writing before the temple's destruction, says it will soon disappear.
